description:
Häagen-Dazs Belgian Chocolate Ice Cream – Homemade & Ultra-Rich 🍨🍫 

Love Häagen-Dazs Belgian Chocolate ice cream? This video shows you how to recreate that deep, intense chocolate flavour and silky-smooth texture at home—using real Belgian chocolate, quality cream, and a few pro tips for that signature finish.
The beauty is, there are NO EGGS in this recipe!

If you’re a chocolate purist, this one’s for you.

📍Chapters:
0:00 Intro
0:39 The ESSENTIAL ingredient
1:28 Making the ice cream base
3:28 Cocoa fact
4:22 The next day, churning and adding in the belgian chocolate
5:35 Scoop and serve
5:50 Final thoughts & tasting notes

Whether you’re recreating your favourite store-bought treat or just exploring how good chocolate ice cream can be, this recipe delivers.

🛒 Full recipe below.
💬 Like, subscribe, and share if you’re serious about your scoop.

#BelgianChocolate #HaagenDazsCopycat #ChocolateIceCream #IceCreamRecipe #FrozenDesserts #FoodScience #HomemadeIceCream


Haagen Dazs Belgian Chocolate Ingredients (makes 2L/2KG): 

840ml Double Cream (Heavy Cream)
640ml Milk
215g Sugar (granulated or caster )
107g Dextrose
200g of 70% Belgian Chocolate
95g of Dark Cocoa Powder
100g Skimmed Milk Powder
2g Stabilzer (Optional)

comments.text:
I'm afraid a big wall of text may dissuade you from reading further so I'll just list my points here:      

1. Using Skim Milk to replace Skim Milk Powder. Where 1 gram of SMP equals 10 grams of Skim Milk.      

2. Protein can denature and clump up when heated, especially so when adding protein powder to liquids.    
In an attempt to circumvent curdled protein I ended up creating a viscous ice cream that had a nice texture and mouth feel.      

3. Using liquid (or other highly concentrated forms of) sweeteners might actually help us get a much better ice cream texture.



I will continue in my own comment, if I have managed to capture's anyone curiousity to help me out.
comments.author: @Titanicunillingus

comments.text:
Summer is coming, Nick. And I need your aid in a most finnicky task. 

I'm aware that you get a ton of questions across all your videos, but I feel like I made a couple "discoveries" or things to consider recently; when making ice creams. 

I'm trying to make a low caloric high protein ice cream. Obviously using the Ninja Creami.

Just to note: I give myself "a budget" of at most 500 calories for a normal pint of Ninja Creami. Which must also contain a protein:calorie ration of 10:100. 
So for every 100 colaries the ice cream offers 10 grams of protein (mininum).

Coming across your channel was a miracle, because 90% of the Ninja Creami content on YT or otherwise is just garbage and made by people that don't know what they're talking about.

So to adress the previous points: 
1. I have a hard time getting SMP. It's not really available anywhere near me. However, I suddenly had a flash of genius where I realized that people used evaporated milk for other recipes for a more dairy intense flavour. Meaning more concentrated milks solids. Meaning that I could do that probably with Skim Milk to achieve the same results as with adding SMP. 
The calculation is simple. 
10 grams of SMP is equal to 100 grams of Skim Milk. 
After adding the Skim Milk we need to heat the base and evaporate 100 grams out of it. Basically "leaving behind the solids of 100 grams of Skim Milk", which is nearly identical to 10 grams of SMP. 

2. So keeping point 1 in mind. I wanted to make a more satisfying Ninja Creami low caloric high protein ice cream. Feeling excited, because I suddenly gained access to a substance I previously thought to be inaccessible to me. 
So I setup a recipe. I can't add Whey Isolate to a hot liquid, because it curdles immediately. The heat denatures the proteins and then the proteins clump together. 
So I blendered 420 grams of 1.5% milk with 60 grams of Whey Isolate. 
I put this in a pan together with: 
200 grams of Skim Milk. 
1 egg yolk 
20 grams of erythritol 
0.5 grams of Guargum (naturally mixed with the erythritol beforehand)

I turned on the stove and tried to evaporate 200 grams out of the ice cream base.

But here it goes wrong; which I had actually imagined could indeed occur. I kept weighing the pan and even though I had not even lost 5 grams of water-weight the base seemed to get thicker. 
I kept going until 20 grams was lost, because at that point it was really thick. 
I took the pan off the stove and kept whisking it until another ~60 grams was lost. 
At this point there is a grainy and filmy type texture to the base. 

After cooling down more the base turned quite thick. I was afraid of putting that in a creami pint and spinning it. 
Not to mention that I had still not gotten rid of the 200 grams of water weight. 

I added ~70 grams of Skim Milk and ~30 grams of water (mixed with coffee because I wanted coffee flavour) and whisked it to make it thinner. This helped a bit.

I didn't want to just chuck away so much stuff so I divided it between 2 pints. It came to about ~370 gram each. 

I put 1 in the freezer and 1 in the fridge. 
The one in the freezer was left overnight for ~12 hours. 
After taking it out I tested with a spoon to see how malleable it was and it seemed soft enough to put it in the machine. 
Just to be sure I still waited 5 minutes and also heated the sides of the pint just in case. 
Then I put it in the machine, hit the Lite Ice Cream button and prayed that my machine wouldn't break before I got to even get a dozen pints out of it. 

The pint came out perfect. With an amazing texture. I was thoroughly surprised by how good the texture was. 

So then I wondered, can this not be used to make really good ice cream textures and bridge the gap between full-fat ice cream and low-caloric "milk" ice creams more (beyond just stabilizers and emulsifers)? 
This is an icecreamery channel so I wanted to ask it here. 
Maybe you already knew all this. Maybe there is a caveat I'm not seeing yet (I haven't tried any more recipes but will soon). 

Thanks to the emulsifiers and stabilizers the ice cream could be put back into the freezer and retrieved later with amazing texture. 

I would love to know whether something as simple as heating up protein-infused milk to create protein-networks and have it "gel up" because of that; could work to increase texture quality. 
I'm guessing a more large-scale version of the protein powder "curdling" happened with the slow heating + whisking method.


3. The third point comes from the above experiment for the 2nd pint. The first pint was lacking sweetness. Flavour and texture were perfect, but sweetness was nowhere to be found. 
The sucralose in the 60 grams of Whey Isolate and the 20 grams of Erythritol wasn't enough. 
Unfortunately I couldn't add more Erythritol because of the 2 side-effects: 
The Freezing Point Depression is 3 times as strong as that of sugar. 
Only a small bit of Erythritol can be absorbed by water, the rest stays out and give crystalline texture to the ice cream. 

But then I realized something. 
I had come across a "liquid sweetener" in a store; of which 5 mL was equivalent to 66 grams of sugar in sweetness. 
So I bought that and added in 8 grams (which was just a tad too much) and ended up with ice cream that was sweet, without altering the ratios and such. 

So what if we can push this to the max? Leave sugar and sweeteners out of the equation. 
The only thing we consider for the texture of ice cream would be Skim Milk Powder and Whey Isolate protein powder. 
Because when/if the texture ends up perfect, all we have to do is add the intense sweetener to our liking, without messing up the ice cream. 
And the ice cream will end up with a more dairy-like flavour (which is what I like about ice cream). 
The FPD and PAC of the solids in the ice cream base needs to be considered as well obviously so we probably have to use some amount of sweetener anyway, but at least we don't have to worry about making the ice cream "sweet enough" with just the crystalline sweeteners alone! 

I'd love to hear your thoughts (and anyone else that has read this far) about that too. 


(PS: does anyone know how to add a nice strong caramel flavour to ice cream without adding calories? Should I look for an extract of some kind or something. I don't have access to allulose).
